subject: calderMobile
pitch:
Category: Abstract.
Subject: hanging mobile.
Style: Alexander Calder.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through a Calder-style abstract hanging mobile built with wires and balanced arms holding colored shapes in red, black, yellow, blue, and white, anchored by a ceiling hook and positioned so it hangs properly above ground level.

I'm leaning toward adding a joint hierarchy -- a root hook joint with child arm joints -- so each arm can rotate naturally like a real mobile, keeping the overall structure around 180-340 lines of code.

Now I'm fleshing out the Calder-style design: flat painted sheet-metal shapes in matte red, black, yellow, blue, and white, with thin black wire rods connecting them and small loop rings at the joints. I'm planning the hierarchy from the top down — a ceiling hook, then a main curved horizontal arm offset from center for visual balance, with pivot points positioned asymmetrically so the mobile hangs naturally.

I'm sketching out a recursive data structure for building the mobile: leaf nodes represent hanging shapes with color and drop-wire length, while arm nodes represent balance bars with left/right spans, tilt, and child nodes. I'm working through how a builder function would create joints and position bones along the vertical axis to construct the whole branching structure programmatically.

Rather than relying on orientation-based posing, I decide to compute each arm's endpoint directly from an azimuth angle and length, giving more control over how the arms splay out in 3D space, and I'm adding a slight tilt parameter to mimic the realistic, gently unbalanced look of real Calder-style mobiles.

For each arm I'm building a wavy wire using a catmull curve through the end, midpoints, and pivot, rendered as a thin dark sweep. At the pivot and at each hanging end I'm adding small torus-shaped eyelets to mimic hooks and loops, connected by straight rods, giving the mobile its characteristic jointed, hand-fabricated look.

Now I'm planning the leaf/plate shapes that hang from the mobile — defining simple 2D outlines like discs and polygons that get extruded into flat shapes, which will dangle as the decorative elements of the piece.

I'll keep the axes orthogonal by rotating the up vector around the yaw axis using an axis-angle rotation, so the tilt stays consistent with the shape's orientation, with the outline drawn relative to the attach point at the origin.

Now I'm defining each mobile shape's outline as a set of points hanging below the origin — disc, leaf, kidney, crescent, triangle, each scaled by size and shaped with its own silhouette.

I'm also considering adding Calder-style spheres hung from wire and small attached discs, making sure polygon outlines like the crescent and blob stay non-self-intersecting while applying smoothing where appropriate.

For the paint treatment, I'm defining a sheet-metal material function that adds subtle mottling and slight edge darkening based on surface normals, so faces and walls read as matte extruded metal rather than flat color.

I could layer simple shapes for decal-like effects instead, like placing a small disc on a larger one, or use coordinate-based paint functions to create concentric ring patterns on a disc for a Calder-esque banded look.

For the mobile's structure, I'm keeping the shapes double-sided and simple, skipping extras like stands or ceiling plates — just a basic hook at the top connecting to the mount. I'm thinking through the overall height scheme, aiming for roughly realistic mobile proportions with the root hook near the top and the lowest element comfortably above the floor, though I'd ideally want to verify this with an actual bounding box calculation once built.

Since I can't easily shift the root after construction, I'm going to carefully plan the drop distances in the tree so the final lowest point lands close to my target. I'm sketching a recursive scheme: each wire drop determines the next pivot's y-position, starting from the hook near the top, then a support wire down to the first arm's pivot, and from there branching into left and right arm segments with specific spans, azimuths, and slight tilts to balance the heavier and lighter sides.

Continuing to work out the mobile's branching structure, I'm assigning each arm's left and right endpoints to either a leaf/ball/disc shape or another sub-arm, computing drop lengths and bottom y-positions for each so the whole thing balances visually and reaches close to the target depth.

Considering adding a small sixth-level arm G with a couple leaves off F's right side. Tallying leaves across the structure gives seven so far: the red leaf, the ball and crescent, the white target, the triangle and yellow blob, and the blue leaf — I want a few more to round out the composition.

Still working out the arm positions...

Working out end positions for A's two arms, then using those to place where C and B hang below, computing B's arm endpoints at its own azimuth to check for spatial overlap with the rest of the structure.

At C, the x-extent feels unbalanced against the leftward spread elsewhere, so I'm reconsidering the azimuth and arm lengths to pull the endpoint back toward center rather than letting it swing too far right.

Continuing the chain down to G, then checking collisions — the white target disc sits clear of B's leaf and support wire, confirming its placement is safe before I move on to positioning the D crescent piece.

The overall bounding box skews right across x -.7 to 1.14, so rather than reposition each element individually, I'll just apply a global offset of -0.2 to the hook's x-coordinate to recenter the whole hanging sculpture around x=0.

Now I'm defining the data types for leaf and arm sub-structures, where each child node tracks its own drop distance (the wire length from its attachment point down to the shape) plus yaw/tilt for orientation. Writing the build function...

Still writing rig geometry...

Still defining arm geometry...

Simplifying the pivot design: the support wire ends right at point P, with a small torus loop encircling the arm there, oriented perpendicular to the arm's direction, and the wire visually joins the top of that loop.

For the joint hierarchy, I'm setting up each arm's joint with its parent link, keeping orientation defaults inherited from the parent since explicit bone assignments handle the rest. Now I'm defining a shape-making function that builds leaf outlines in unit scale anchored at their attachment point.

Writing outline generators...

Computing where the blob attaches near the top, settling on center y=-0.9. Now I'm working out a crescent shape using two overlapping arcs, outer radius 1 and inner radius 0.7 offset horizontally, opening the crescent upward toward its attachment point.

Working out the inner arc radius and angle sweep so the crescent's two circles meet smoothly at the endpoints...

For the triangle shape I'm thinking it should hang from one sharp vertex with an asymmetric tilt, keeping all corners sharp with no smoothing, mimicking Calder's style. I'm also considering adding a thin wedge shape alongside the six main shapes plus the ball to round out the mobile's variety.

Now I'm working through the extrusion parameters—scaling outline coordinates, setting attachment points, and tuning smoothing per shape based on point count and concavity, since smoothing can fail on shapes with crossing cut corners like the crescent's concave inner edge. I'm settling on a sheet-metal-like thickness around 0.006-0.008 to match Calder's scaled proportions.

For the attachment point, I'm adding a small eyelet torus near the top where the hanging wire connects, positioning it slightly offset from the shape's top corner so the wire end sits naturally above it. I'm also thinking through paint/color application per shape and considering slight yaw rotation so each leaf's normal faces the right direction, then moving on to defining spherical balls with a size-based radius.

Now I'm setting up the hung sphere pieces with low-poly flat-shaded geometry, attaching them below their wire anchor point, and sketching out a small cylindrical cap ring at the top attachment with simple flat or mottled paint. I'm also laying out the Calder-inspired color palette -- cadmium red, near-black, mustard yellow, deep blue, and off-white -- to use across the mobile's shapes.

Writing sheet paint function...

Still writing paint shader logic...

For attaching the disc to the leaf surface, I can use the shape's local-to-model point conversion to position it right at the face, offset slightly along the thickness axis so it sits flush. I'll wrap this into a generic inlay option that takes a shape, scale, position, and color for easy reuse.

Then I'm thinking about adding a hook at the top — maybe a small torus loop plus a short wire, to make the piece hangable like a mobile.

Still shaping the hook geometry...

For eyelets at the arm ends, I'm placing a small torus loop slightly offset outward from the endpoint, oriented so its plane sits along the arm direction with a perpendicular axis, letting the next wire hook through it naturally.

Defining the type interfaces...

Setting up imports from the builder SDK and sketching a hang function for positioning nodes relative to a parent point...

Still writing hang function logic...

Still computing arm endpoints...

For eyelets I'm defining a small torus geometry with reduced segments for a faceted look, oriented along the local axis at each attach point. I'm also writing a recursive helper that places a wire loop at the end of each branch and offsets downward to spawn the hanging child element.

Now I'm setting up the leaf orientation math, computing the yaw-rotated X axis and tilting the Y axis around it so the leaf's face normal points the right direction.

I'm extruding the leaf outline along these axes into a thin bevelled shape, using a small bevel size and per-shape smoothing settings, then attaching an eyelet at the connection point using the cross product of the X and Y axes as the normal.

For the eyelet geometry, I'm positioning a torus slightly above the top so it pokes partially through the sheet shape while the wire end extends straight upward from there.

Now I'm setting up a helper that scales outline point arrays while preserving the "sharp" corner markers, and defining a point type to match the outline format expected by the builder library, casting as needed for TypeScript compatibility.

Then I'm defining the actual shapes—disc, oval, leaf, blob, crescent, triangle, wedge—each with their own point counts and smoothing values, with the leaf shape using sharp tips at the top and bottom and curved sides in between.

Now I'm sketching out the tree structure itself: a hook point, a root arm "armA" with specific angle, length, and tilt parameters, branching into "armB" and "armC" with their own drop values, and attaching leaf decorations at the branch ends.

Computing pivot and endpoint y-coordinates for each arm segment to verify leaves stay within valid height bounds after accounting for sway and tilt adjustments.

Let me reconsider the blue shape for this branch—an oval instead of a leaf since red already has that shape, sizing it around .22-.24 for a height near .44-.48, giving a top around 1.62 and working out the bottom from there.

Now I'm continuing down the arm chain, computing drop offsets and tilt angles for armE and armF, placing a white/red target disc and a black triangle with red inlay, and tracking the resulting top and bottom y-coordinates to check they stay in range.

Moving on to armG, placing a yellow-striped blob and a small white ball, I estimate the lowest point lands around 0.43 against a total height of 3.0, which seems fine, though I want to double-check clearance between the blob and nearby elements before finalizing.

Checking F.A's position against the triangle, confirming no overlap with the disc since the x-coordinate separation holds. Looking at the blue oval and red leaf positions, they're far enough apart to avoid collision, and I'm tracing the support wires to see if they intersect the target disc.

I'm assigning distinct yaw rotations to each shape for visual variety, then working out the overall layout width after offsetting. For the inlay details, I'm computing the triangle's centroid to place a small red disc inlay inside it, scaling the coordinates and adjusting the inlay's size and vertical origin.

I'm figuring out how to position additional inlays—like a yellow disc on the blue oval—using local coordinate frames for each extruded part, keeping bevels off and thickness minimal for these inset details.

Now I'm setting up the color palette and defining paint sheets for each hue, then working out how to build a radial ring paint function that blends two colors based on distance from center for the target-style leaf design.

I'm deciding wire parts just use string colors while arms stay metal-toned, skipping extra decorative beads since Calder's fixed counterweights aren't needed here. I'll name the piece "Calder Mobile" with its own description, setting up the builder with default paint sizing.

For the hanging ring and hook, I'm placing a small torus at the top of the hook point, then sweeping a curved path upward through the ring to form the J-shaped hook, keeping it attached to the root bone with a thin radius.

I'm making the hook itself the root joint, with the arm hanging down from the ring's bottom point, and double-checking that the rod-drawing signature takes the color argument right after the radius.

Writing wire and eyelet geometry...

For safety I'll create a new geometry each call rather than sharing, and add a smaller torus for the leaf attachment rings. I'm weighing whether to pose leaves with slight tilt or let yaw handle it naturally, and considering small extra touches like painted dark arms or a mid-wire bead to give the hanging wires more Calder-like character with subtle kinks.

Setting up helper functions for degrees and vectors, then writing the sweep logic for a slightly offset S-curve wire path using a Catmull-Rom spline between four points. I'm defining the paint/sheet shading function that mixes a base color toward black and white to create primer tones.

Writing arm and leaf definitions...

Still writing wire geometry...

I need to check the sides option for the sweep, then move to the branch logic, arm details, and leaf type definitions with inlay shapes, and make sure smoothing values differ correctly between leaf and other shapes.

Now I'm defining a scaling helper for points, then building the crescent shape by tracing an outer arc and an inner arc, checking whether the endpoints of these two arcs line up closely enough to avoid a tiny degenerate edge.

I'm also working through the blob and oval shapes' point generation, noting that different shapes use opposite winding directions (clockwise vs counterclockwise), and deciding to normalize all shapes to a consistent counterclockwise orientation so the extrusion logic handles them uniformly.

Then I verify the triangle and wedge vertex orderings are also counterclockwise, think through z-offset placement for inlays to avoid collisions, and start writing the final extrusion code for the inlay discs, placing them at local positions with alternating sign offsets along the thickness axis.

Simplifying to disc-only inlays, I'm working out the local coordinate placement, the torus eyelet axis via cross product, the arm pivot torus center, and the loop and hook ring orientations before writing out the complete code.
